# krill — Product brief

This file is the index. Vision, Personas, Load-bearing decisions, Non-goals, and Notes are inline; the three sections with no natural ceiling are split out (`tools/project-manager/CONVENTIONS.md` § Layout):

| Section | File |
|---|---|
| Current state | [`product/01-current-state.md`](product/01-current-state.md) |
| Capability map | [`product/02-capability-map.md`](product/02-capability-map.md) |
| Roadmap | [`product/03-roadmap.md`](product/03-roadmap.md) |

## Vision

Krill is the spec-of-record and work-tracking substrate for agent swarms — **unifying all the personas the way Jira did for humans, except for agents.** Today a product's requirements are flat markdown read cold in one pass and its work lives in GitHub Issues, Discussions, and Projects; nearly every convention the `project-manager` pipeline carries (zero FRs in a brief, doc-splitting thresholds, drafts hidden in gists, "the last ledger comment wins") is a workaround for that shape, and GitHub's rate limits cap how many agents can run against it at once. Krill replaces *read the document* with *query the slice you need*: requirements, decisions, and work become typed entities with history, so an agent receives exactly the context its task requires and nothing else, and the markdown everyone reads today becomes a generated projection rather than the source. A year out it is three things at once — a console a Swarm Operator checks, a platform requirements get shaped on, and the surface agents actually perform work through.

## Personas

- **Swarm Operator** — the admin who wants to see everything and occasionally needs to bang a wrench on it: what is claimed, what is stuck, what dead-lettered, and what to do about it.
- **Requirement Contributor** — someone with no interest in operating the swarm who wants to add to the natural-language requirements. The mental model is the uncle with an idea for the app who cannot write code; the entity model must never be his problem.
- **Agent** — the generic worker persona: needs to know what its task is, what its success condition is, and exactly the right amount of information — no more.

## Load-bearing decisions

LB1 — Scope is a surrogate key, and it is on every row from M1
At risk: C22 (second repo/tenant), C23 (decisions spanning several products) — both
  `Later`; C9 (the GitHub pointer artifact) needs somewhere to hang forge coordinates.
  Decide now: every entity row carries a non-null `scope_id` FK from M1, and the `scope`
  table — not the entity rows — owns the forge coordinates (`repo_full_name`, default
  branch, pointer-issue number). One seeded row in M1, no UI exposes it, but every
  uniqueness constraint and every query predicate is scope-qualified from day one.
  Stays cheap: the scope selector, scope CRUD, per-scope authorization, cross-scope reads,
  and whether a scope is a repo or an org — those are handlers and policy.
  Why the indirection, not just a `repo_full_name` column: with a natural key, a repo
  rename is a rewrite of every row, and C23 (a decision above any single product) has no
  place to live at all. With a surrogate, both are a row edit.

LB2 — Entity identity: immutable surrogate ids, and display numbers are rendered, never stored
At risk: C5/C6 (as-of reads and supersession — an id must outlive the revision that
  minted it), C7 (generated docs cite `FR4`/`LB3`/`C7` by number), C8 (import must
  round-trip), C21 (drift detection compares by identity).
  Decide now: the chain is `Product → FeatureSet → Feature → {FR, NFR}` and
  `FeatureSet → LoadBearingDecision`, strict single-parent, parent FK as a column on the
  child — never an array, never a join table. Each entity has (a) an immutable surrogate
  id, stable across every supersession, and (b) a human-facing display number derived
  per-render and scoped to its parent, which is *not* a stored key.
  Stays cheap: adding new entity kinds under Feature; display-number format; a later
  many-to-many for LoadBearingDecision specifically (C23) — it is a leaf nobody walks
  *through*, so widening it does not touch the scoped query.
  The trap this closes: if `FR4` is the primary key, inserting an FR between 3 and 4, or
  superseding one, renumbers its siblings — and every citation in every generated doc,
  code comment, and CI check that greps for it. `AGENTS.md`'s own splitting rules lean on
  numbered citations staying grep-discoverable across moves. Renumbering is the migration.

LB3 — SCD2 is the spec axis's mutation pattern; the work axis is append-only + claimed
At risk: C5 (value at time T), C6 (supersede, never overwrite), C15/C17/C18 (a run's
  attempt history, dead-letter state, and operator intervention are all work-axis writes).
  Decide now: spec entities are SCD2 per `AGENTS.md` § SCD2 — `valid_from`/`valid_to`,
  partial index on `valid_to IS NULL`, as-of via the window-function form. Work-axis
  tables (task/queue rows, claims, leases, attempts, run records, notes) are append-only
  or append-only-plus-claimed and explicitly **not** SCD2, matching the shipped precedent
  in `tools/app_registry/migrate/schema/migrations/004_writeback_outbox.up.sql` and
  `AGENTS.md`'s own "Do not apply SCD2 to append-only event logs." The boundary is drawn
  per table in M1 and written into the schema comments.
  Stays cheap: which columns an entity carries, new entity kinds, offloading superseded
  bodies to S3, deriving an SCD2-shaped *view* over a work table with `LEAD(...) OVER`
  if a consumer ever wants one.
  This contradicts the intake's "Mutation. SCD2 throughout." See open question 6 — I am
  reading that as "throughout the spec axis," and if it was meant literally it needs
  re-deciding before M1, not after.

LB4 — Every mutation records two subjects, in the shape already shipped in this repo
At risk: C24 (attribute an action to an agent identity, not just to a run) — `Later`;
  C15/C17/C18 (who ran it, who is stuck, who intervened).
  Decide now: every mutating call records an **acting** identity and an **on-behalf-of**
  identity, each as `(iss, sub, kind)` with `iss` a real column, both always populated
  (`on_behalf_of = acting` when the credential carries no delegation).
  Both subjects are DERIVED server-side from the caller's verified credential, never client-supplied, by a pure function shared by the MCP server and the api binary.
  M1's "the acting subject is the human who called init" is superseded.
  Delegation is described generically: a credential MAY carry a delegation (a delegate acting for a principal); then acting is the delegate (kind agent)
  and on-behalf-of is the principal (kind human). Each front door maps its own credential shape onto that pair; the whagent JWKS door is one such mapping, not the model.
  Derivable kinds are human, agent and service (service comes from an OIDC service-account token).
  No service may assert another identity: krill/ui forwards the operator's own Keycloak token and the api verifies it; there is no service-asserted exception.
  Stays cheap: authorization policy (read-vs-control is a rule, not a schema); per-scope authorization; run-id TTL; revocation.
  Why this keeps C24 cheap: the two columns already exist and are populated from the credential's own delegation, so an agent identity is a value in an existing column.

LB5 — Krill owns an FR's identity; committed docs are one-way projections with provenance
At risk: C7 (generated read-only docs), C8 (import), C21 (drift detection) — C21 is not
  merely enabled by this, it is *computable only because of* it.
  Decide now: the direction of ownership, from M1. Krill's surrogate id (LB2) is the
  identity of an FR; a rendered file is a projection carrying a header naming the entity
  and the render revision it came from. Nothing ever parses a committed doc back into
  krill except the one-time importer (C8), which is a separate, deliberately one-way code
  path with no reverse.
  Stays cheap: when rendering runs (hook, schedule, manual), split thresholds and file
  naming (renderer config), whether a render lands as a PR or a push, drift tolerance
  windows, and the `AGENTS.md` carve-out itself.
  Why it is load-bearing and not a preference: two writable sources makes the reconciler a
  permanent tax rather than a temporary one, and the reverse direction is unpickable —
  the first hand-edit to a generated file that someone expects to survive turns "generated"
  into "merged," and there is no migration back.

LB6 — The delivery axis is an association, never a second parent
At risk: C13 (milestones and milepebbles as a separate axis), C6 (an FR must outlive the
  milestone that shipped it, for "truncate, never rewind" to mean anything), C14/C15
  (the entire work axis hangs off delivery, not off the spec chain).
  Decide now: M1 ships the spec chain only — but the moment it records *any* delivery
  notion, including "shipped in M1" on the migrated conformance product, that is a row in
  an association table keyed `(entity_id, milestone_id)`, never a `milestone_id` column on
  FR or Feature.
  Stays cheap: milepebble granularity, the status set (including `partially complete`),
  whether one FR may appear in two milestones, re-cutting a milestone, and the whole work
  surface built on top.
  The failure this avoids: a `milestone_id` column makes the *when* axis a second parent
  in a chain LB2 declares single-parent. Unpicking it later is a migration of every
  requirement row plus a rewrite of the scoped query that walks the chain.

LB7 — The scoped slice is one versioned document, and it is what a claim payload later carries
At risk: C14 (a self-contained claim payload the worker never supplements) and C16
  (resume on any host) — both `Next`; C19 (a UI reading the same thing).
  Decide now: C3's scoped query returns a typed, self-describing document — an explicit
  schema version, plus the entity ids and the as-of revisions it was assembled from — and
  M1's MCP tool (C4) is a thin wrapper over it, not the thing itself.
  Stays cheap: adding fields to the document, the verb set's payload contents, lane
  sequences, cap values, routing, and which fields any given consumer reads.
  Why M1 decides this even though the work surface is `Next`: the claim payload's core
  *is* this slice. Built as a typed document, the work surface is enrichment. Built as a
  tool response shaped for an interactive reader, the work surface needs a second
  projection of the same data, and the two drift — which is `whagent_net`'s LB1 ("the same
  record, not three projections") learned the expensive way.

## Non-goals

**Permanent:**

- **Writing code.** Krill does requirement gathering, planning, triage, and spec-of-record maintenance. Code execution stays with whatever harness runs it.
- **Being a general-purpose issue tracker for humans.** Krill unifies personas around agent work; it is not where humans file bugs.
- **Pluggable storage backends.** One backend, many harnesses. Making a forge (gitea, GitHub) able to back krill would mean keeping issues, comments, and labels as the lowest common denominator — throwing away the typed structure that is the entire point. *This is about what krill is **stored in**, not about who it serves: it does not conflict with C22, which puts a second repo or tenant on the same instance and the same single backend.*
- **Owning git.** The forge keeps owning the repository and the merge.
- **Orchestrating or dispatching agents.** Krill hands out work and records what came back; spawning, scheduling, and supervising agent runs belong to the harness.
- **Rendering anything but the product doc set.** C7's renderer owns `PRODUCT.md` and `product/*` and nothing else. `ARCHITECTURE.md` is not in scope and is not a deferral either — *architecture always lives with the code, as it is the essence of how the code is implemented; product is the first pass.* `README.md`, `ENV.md`, and `TOC.md` likewise stay hand-written. This keeps the `AGENTS.md` carve-out for generated docs narrow: only product docs become non-hand-editable. Revisitable eventually, but not v1 and probably not v2.

**Explicitly *not* non-goals — deferred, not foreclosed:**

- **A web UI.** In the vision, not in v1 (C19). An API-only console closes M5.
- **Owning branch and PR lifecycle.** v1 stores references only — M4 holds them as rows, per its first recorded condition — and owning the lifecycle later is plausible and must not be designed out (C20), protected by that same condition: krill never derives task state from a branch name.
- **Multi-repo / multi-tenant use.** One repo in practice; scope is carried on every row from M1 (LB1) so this is later a matter of handlers and auth.

## Notes

Notes recorded against this Product in krill, oldest first. The status after each id is the note's own lifecycle status (`store.NoteLifecycleStatus`); anything other than `noted` is rendered for the record, not as current fact.

# Reparent coverage beyond Feature — decided per entity kind

The correction-surface milepebble scoped reparenting to `Feature` only (`store.ReparentStore.ReparentFeature`, MCP `reparent_feature`). This records, per parent link, whether the other four need a move verb. The criterion used throughout is not "is a move possible" but **"does create-and-retire leave a dangling citation in the rendered record or in another table's key?"** — if yes, the entity needs a verb that keeps its id; if no, create-and-retire is correct and a verb would be a second way to do a rarer thing.

## `feature_set` (parent: `product_id`) — NO. Create-and-retire is correct.

A FeatureSet move is a *product* move, and it is the same failure `ReparentStore` already refuses with `ErrReparentAcrossProduct`, one level up. A FeatureSet's children carry `display_number`s allocated by `position.go`'s `nextDisplayNumber`, which is deliberately **product-wide** (migration 017; it MAXes over every row of the table in the product, unfiltered on the parent's currentness). A milestone's rendered `Delivers: Cn` line resolves a citation by looking the entity up *in the slice of the product it is rendering*. So re-homing a FeatureSet under a different product would carry its Features' and LoadBearingDecisions' `Cn`/`LBn` values into a second numbering space while every existing citation to them stays in the first — the cited item would silently drop out of the `Delivers` line of the milestone that delivers it. A supersede cannot fix that, because the numbers are not the thing being changed. Void the FeatureSet, recreate it under the right product. The advice `AmendPlacementChange.placementAdvice` already gives is right, and this note is the reason behind it.

## `requirement` (parent: `feature_id`) — NO. Create-and-retire is correct, and it is cheap.

Requirements are the one parent link with no cross-cutting cost to breaking. `nextDisplayNumber` is called only for `"feature"` and `"load_bearing_decision"` (`store/feature.go`, `store/decision.go`, `store/mediated.go`) — a Requirement has no `display_number` at all, so nothing in the rendered record cites one. Nothing keys on `Requirement.feature_id` either: `entity_milestone`/`delivery_shipment` key on `entity_id` (in practice a Feature or LoadBearingDecision `Cn`/`LBn`), and `task` keys on `milestone_id`. Recreate the requirement under the correct Feature and `void` the old one; the void tombstone keeps the old id resolvable, so a stale citation in prose or a task body resolves to a visibly voided requirement rather than to a different live one — the same guarantee void already gives everywhere. The only cost is a new id for a requirement whose text was simply filed under the wrong parent, and the correction path for that is cheap enough not to justify a ninth verb. Worth stating explicitly because the absence was never a decision anyone recorded.

## `milestone` where the move is `product_id` — NO. Create-and-retire is correct.

Same `Cn`-numbering argument as FeatureSet, and stronger: a milestone's own `Delivers` rows are the citations that resolve through the *old* product's slice. Re-homing one would strand them. `abandon_milestone` + create under the right product is the answer; `store.abandon.go`'s own "truncate, never rewind" note already frames the abandoned milestone as a readable record.

## `milestone` where the move is `parent_milestone_id` (a milepebble between milestones) — **YES. This is a real, bounded gap, and the current advice is a bad one.**

This is the one case where the answer is yes, and the reasoning is the exact inverse of the two no's above: the move stays *inside* one product's numbering space, so no `Cn` or `LBn` citation dangles, and the milepebble's `id` — which every one of its tasks, status events, deferrals, and `Delivers` rows hangs off — survives. It is a single-column supersede on an already-SCD2 table (migration 020), going through the same `supersede` helper `ReparentFeature` uses, differing only in that `parent_milestone_id` is what differs. The move is also a real and recurring correction: "this cut actually belongs to M3, not M2" is a routine outcome of working a milestone.

What makes today's advice (`placementAdvice`, and the equivalent in `Refuse`): *"create the milepebble under the milestone you want, then abandon_milestone this one"* — genuinely bad for this case. It discards the milepebble's id, its entire task list, its status history, and its deferrals, and strands the completed work in the backlog bucket. For a milepebble that is three-quarters done that is not a correction, it is a data-loss event with extra steps.

Two conditions a future verb must honour, both already expressible with machinery that exists:
- FR3's subset invariant. The destination milestone must already deliver everything the milepebble delivers, or the move expands the destination's committed scope as a side effect. `MilestoneAuthoringStore.AddMilepebbleDelivers` (`getMilepebbleParent` + the parent `Delivers` check) is the existing expression of this check.
- It moves `milestone_ref.parent_milestone_id` only. It touches no `entity_milestone` row — the milepebble keeps its own `Delivers` associations — so it is not the `entity_milestone` correction surface, which is a separate question recorded separately.

Recommended shape, for whoever picks this up: `store.ReparentStore.ReparentMilepebble(ctx, id, parentMilestoneID)` beside `ReparentFeature`, with a `ErrReparentAcrossProduct`-analogue refused for a `kind='milestone'` row (a milestone has no parent milestone; `getMilepebbleParent`'s `errNotAMilepebble` is the existing named refusal), plus an `ErrMilepebbleDeliversNotSubset` reuse. MCP: `reparent_milepebble` in the same place `reparent_feature` is registered. This is small — it is the shape `ed45c9ec` already landed, applied to a different column.

## Summary table

| Parent link | Move verb? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `feature` → `feature_set_id` | **Exists** (`reparent_feature`) | `Cn` is product-wide and cited everywhere; a move must keep the id |
| `milestone_ref` (kind=`milepebble`) → `parent_milestone_id` | **Yes, missing** | stays in one product's numbering space; keeps the id its tasks/history hang off; current advice is destructive |
| `feature_set` → `product_id` | No | moves its children's `Cn`/`LBn` across a numbering boundary; create-and-retire |
| `requirement` → `feature_id` | No | no `display_number`, no foreign key keys on it; void+recreate is cheap and the tombstone keeps stale citations honest |
| `milestone` (kind=`milestone`) → `product_id` | No | its own `Delivers: Cn` lines resolve in the old product's slice; abandon+create |

The two "no"s on cross-product moves are not a preference for the status quo: they are forced by `nextDisplayNumber`'s product-wide allocation combined with the renderer resolving `Delivers` citations through one product's slice. The same coupling is what `ReparentStore`'s own comment cites for `ErrReparentAcrossProduct`; this note generalises it to the two links it does not yet cover.

No code was changed for this note. It records decisions only; `ReparentMilepebble` is explicitly not built here.

# The `milestone_deferral` SCD2 reversal: fact-with-revisions, not a fact with an amendment log

Consequence #1 of the reversal recorded in the note against LB3 (`c0329287-3b3a-45fb-b4b0-96ea926f2fe4`) and implemented by this milepebble's `AmendDeferral` task. That note records *that* the reversal happened and why migration 010's "a deferral is a fact, not a value that changes over time" was half-right — it holds for the deferral's *existence*, it did not hold for its *text*. This note records the consequence that note leaves open.

## Decision: keep the current shape. A deferral is a fact-with-revisions.

Recommendation, with the reasoning, because the distinction was left open rather than settled:

**1. History alone already answers the question, in the shape we have.** Each SCD2 revision carries its own `valid_from`/`valid_to` and its own `body`/`destination`. "What was deferred, and when was it corrected" is answerable by ordering one deferral's revisions on `valid_from` and reading each one: revision 1 is what was said at deferral time, revision *n* is what is true now, and the `valid_to` of each is the moment it stopped being said. An amendment log would store the *same* information in a strictly worse shape — a current row plus a parallel log that has to be folded to reconstruct the current value, which is two sources of truth that can disagree, and a reader who has to trust the fold.

**2. The SCD2 shape is the spec axis's uniform mutation pattern (LB3), and reusing it is what keeps the code small.** `store.supersede` is one helper: lock the current row, close it, open the successor, all in one transaction. The partial unique index on `(id) WHERE valid_to IS NULL` is what makes two concurrent amends serialize instead of both winning. Every read path filters `valid_to IS NULL` and every one of them is already written that way for `milestone_ref` and the seven migration-002 tables. An amendment log is a *second, novel* mutation pattern on the delivery axis, needing its own concurrency story and its own reader-side fold — reintroducing on `milestone_deferral` precisely the inconsistency this milepebble set out to remove.

**3. The renderer is read-only and must stay so.** `render.Source.ListMilestoneDeferrals` delegates to `store.ListDeferrals`. Under the SCD2 shape it inherits "current rows only" for free, and the renderer keeps its one-way read direction with no fold logic. Under an amendment log, the fold would have to land somewhere — and the only place it could land is the renderer, which is exactly the direction this codebase refuses to move.

## What "the current shape" commits us to saying about `destination`

Worth being explicit, because it is the part that is not just text. `destination` is NOT NULL and FR1 makes it a claim: "this went to M4" or "this went to the `Later` bucket". Amending a `destination` is therefore rewriting a *routing* claim, not polishing prose — and that is correct and needed, because a re-cut (`RecutStore.MoveScope`) can move the thing a deferral pointed at after the deferral was written. The closed revision is what keeps this honest: it preserves what was claimed *at the time*, so a reader can see a deferral that said M4 and a later correction that said M6, instead of one row whose text silently disagrees with a month of delivery history. Do not treat a deferral's history as a list of mistakes; it is a list of decisions that were true when made.

## Rider: the subject pair on the successor row (open in the implementing task)

`AmendDeferral`'s task leaves this to the implementer ("Decide and document whether the successor row carries the closed row's `created_by_*` forward, or records a new subject pair"). It bears directly on "reconstruct from history alone", so the recommendation, for the same reason: **record a new subject pair — the amender.** Every other amend in the package does, and consistency is not the only argument: with the amender on the current row and the original author on the closed one, both questions ("who first wrote this deferral" and "who corrected it, and when") are answerable from the revisions alone. Carrying the original pair forward would make the second question unanswerable, because two subjects would collapse onto one column. This is a recommendation, not an override — the implementing task owns the decision and should say so in its method comment either way.

## The "which other tables?" question, answered in the negative

The consequence worth writing down is *which axis to draw*, because the naive form of the question ("do the other non-SCD2 content tables need the same treatment for the same reason?") invites an over-application. The reason the deferral's reversal was right is narrow: **a current-value row whose authored text goes stale.** That describes `milestone_deferral` and nothing else on the delivery axis.

- `milestone_status_event` (migration 012) — correctly non-SCD2, and its comment already says so. A status is an event register, not a value; a wrong status is corrected by recording the correct transition, never by editing the past one. Migration 012 goes further and stores no "current status" column at all — current status is *derived* from the event history. Leave it alone.
- `delivery_shipment` (migration 013) — correctly non-SCD2. A shipment is a fact about what was delivered; NFR3's "truncate, never rewind" is the governing rule and an amend would contradict it outright.
- `entity_milestone` (migrations 004/010) — **this one is a different case entirely and needs a different primitive.** It is not a stale-text row and must not be given the same SCD2 treatment. Recorded separately as a scope-note, because it is a real gap with a bounded fix.

No code changed here; this records a decision.

**`af5bf927-1de5-46d6-ad27-84094d5c92ac`** — scope-note — status: noted

# Gap: `entity_milestone` has no correction path for a wrong association — needs a milepebble of its own

Raised by the `milestone_deferral` SCD2 reversal: that reversal asked whether the *other* non-SCD2 content tables need the same treatment. Answer: **`entity_milestone` is a real gap, but it must NOT be fixed the same way.** This note records the finding and the recommended shape. Nothing here is built; no verb was added.

## The gap, stated plainly

`entity_milestone` is a bare append-only table — `id`, `scope_id`, `entity_id`, `milestone_id`, `relation` — with no `valid_from`/`valid_to` (migration 004; the `relation` discriminator is migration 010). Grepping every `DELETE FROM entity_milestone` in `krill/store/` returns **exactly one site**, `recut.go`'s `MoveScope`, and that method is hard-scoped to `relation = 'delivers'`.

So: **a `Must not foreclose:` row naming the wrong capability has no correction path at all.** Not an amend, not a move, not a delete — nothing in the package, and therefore nothing on the MCP mount. The same shape of gap the deferral had (append-only, no correction path, a content claim that turns out to be wrong), in a table nobody has named.

## Which corrections are already covered, so this is not a bigger hole than it looks

Checked against the code rather than assumed:

- **Wrong milestone on an unshipped `Delivers` row — already correctable.** `RecutStore.MoveScope` (MCP `move_delivery_scope`) re-points a `delivers` association between any two `milestone_ref` rows, including into the backlog bucket. It refuses only shipped items (`ErrEntityShipped`), items the `from` container does not deliver (`ErrEntityNotInContainer`), and the one move that would leave two milestone-level owners (`ErrEntityDeliveredBySiblingCut`). The real gap here is a **framing** gap, not a code gap: MoveScope was built and documented as the *re-cut* primitive ("move a milestone's not-yet-shipped scope to a different milestone"), and nothing in its doc comment says it is also the correction path for a delivery decision that was recorded against the wrong milestone. Worth a sentence in its doc comment, at minimum.
- **An already-shipped association — correctly not correctable.** `ErrEntityShipped` is NFR3's "truncate, never rewind" enforced, and it is right. A shipped association is history; the correction is a new commitment elsewhere, not an edit. This is a "no", not part of the gap.
- **`must_not_foreclose` — no path whatsoever.** The gap.
- **Wrong *entity* (delivers `C13` when the truth is `C28`) — no direct path, awkward workaround.** `MoveScope` moves an association between containers, not between entities. The only route is two calls: move the wrong association to the backlog, then `add_delivers` the right one. That leaves the product's backlog bucket holding an item that was never backlogged and never shipped, which is a false claim about product state — arguably worse than the original error. Part of the gap.

## Why SCD2 is the wrong fix here, and must not be applied

The temptation is to extend the deferral's reversal: "`entity_milestone` is also non-SCD2, so make it SCD2 too." **Do not.** The deferral's reversal was right because a deferral is a *current-value row whose authored text goes stale*. An `entity_milestone` row is neither that nor an append-only event register — it is an **edge**, and its correction is a *withdrawal*, not a revision. Concretely:

- SCD2 on an edge table means every edge can exist in a "current" and a "closed" state, so "does milestone M deliver C7?" becomes a query that must filter, on a table whose whole job is to answer that question in one join. Every read of `entity_milestone` (in `krill/slice`, `krill/render`, `krill/store`'s `GetMilestone`) would have to learn about validity, and the renderer's `Delivers:` line would gain a filter it should never need.
- The information an SCD2 chain would hold is exactly what one nullable column already holds: *this edge was withdrawn, by whom, at what time*. A `withdrawn_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL` + `withdrawn_by_*` (NFR4's subject pair, as `milestone_ref`/`task` already carry) on the existing append-only rows, with current = `withdrawn_at IS NULL`, is the same information at a fraction of the read-path cost and with no risk of a reader forgetting the filter.
- It also keeps the write honest in the way NFR3 needs: withdrawing an edge is a *new fact about the present*, recorded once, and the withdrawal itself is what history shows.

So the axis to draw when someone asks "does this table need the deferral's treatment?" is: **current-value row with authored text → SCD2. Append-only event/fact register → leave alone, correct by recording a new event. Edge/association → a withdrawal column, not `valid_from`/`valid_to`.** `entity_milestone` is the first table in krill to land in the third bucket.

## Recommended shape, and why it is bounded

One verb covering both relations, on `MilestoneAuthoringStore` or a new sibling beside `RecutStore`:

```
WithdrawAssociation(ctx, scopeID, milestoneID, entityID uuid.UUID, relation MilestoneRelation, acting, onBehalfOf Subject) error
```

- Refuses, writing nothing, if the row does not exist (nothing to withdraw — distinct from the idempotent no-op case, which should be loud here the way `ErrReparentNoOp` is), if the entity is already shipped in that milestone (`ErrEntityShipped`, reusing the existing refusal rather than inventing a near-duplicate), and if `relation` is neither `delivers` nor `must_not_foreclose` (the CHECK constraint already rejects it, so this is belt-and-braces at the tool layer).
- Writes a `withdrawn_at` + subject pair; never deletes. MCP: `withdraw_delivery_association` beside `move_delivery_scope` in `krill/mcp/tools/recut.go`, same persona list.
- The `delivers` half is mostly a **refactor**: the tombstone write and the shipped check both already exist inside `MoveScope`'s transaction, so the new method is largely an extraction plus the "withdraw in place" half that `MoveScope` does not have (it always re-inserts at a destination).
- The `must_not_foreclose` half is genuinely new, and it is small: a tombstone write and a shipped check, both mirroring what already exists.

## Disposition

**Yes — this is real, and it should become its own milepebble**, not a task folded into `correction-surface-gaps`. It is a different axis from the spec axis this milepebble spent itself on: it is a change to the delivery axis's mutation model (an edge gains a current/withdrawn dimension it has never had), it carries a schema change, and it has a design decision in front of it — the withdrawal column — that the reparent work had no reason to consider. Folding it in would smuggle a schema-and-model change into a milepebble whose stated scope is the spec axis's correction surface, and the existing `correction-surface-gaps` cut is already carrying five tasks.

Suggested milepebble shape: **"Delivery-association correction surface"** — the withdrawal column, `withdraw_delivery_association`, and the `MoveScope` doc-comment correction naming it as the correction path too. It does not depend on anything in `correction-surface-gaps` except sharing the `ErrEntityShipped` refusal, and it blocks nothing in it.

No code was written for this note.

**`e9f46b5b-395f-4da8-9d13-f57328a6eb86`** — comment — status: noted

# CORRECTION — the subject-pair rider was wrong; the decision is made and shipped as carry-forward

**This note supersedes the rider in `e697a0ef-c8aa-4f5e-a55e-f43f67dc89d5`.** That rider is withdrawn. Its conclusion was the opposite of what shipped, and it described the question as still open when it was not. Read this note instead of that paragraph; everything else in `e697a0ef` (the fact-with-revisions recommendation) stands unchanged.

## The decision, as made and shipped

Task `6a10030d-b53c-4540-8d6c-fc08d6d9df67`, commit `3a3e2f54`, `krill/store/amend.go:264-296`. The successor row **carries the closed row's `created_by_acting` / `created_by_on_behalf_of` forward**. It does not record the amender's own subject pair.

Verified in the code, not inferred from the commit message: the INSERT at `amend.go:295-296` passes `current.CreatedByActing.Iss`, `current.CreatedByActing.Sub`, `string(current.CreatedByActing.Kind)`, and the three `CreatedByOnBehalfOf` equivalents — the closed row's values, not the amender's. It also passes `current.CreatedAt` forward for the same reason. The doc comment above it states the choice and the reason: those columns name *who deferred the item*, a fact about when it was deferred, which does not change when its wording is corrected.

This is the `milestone_ref` convention, not a one-off. `AmendMilestone` does the same thing through `subjectArgs(current.CreatedByActing)` / `subjectArgs(current.CreatedByOnBehalfOf)` / `current.CreatedAt`. So the rule is uniform across the milestone table and its deferrals: **an amend never rewrites who created the thing.**

## Why my earlier recommendation was wrong

I recommended recording the amender's pair instead, and my stated reason was that carrying it forward "would make the second question unanswerable, because two subjects would collapse onto one column." That reason is simply false, and the error in it is worth naming because it is a general trap: I treated the current row's `created_by_*` columns as the *only* place a subject could be recorded, so a pair that does not change with each revision looked like it was losing information.

It is not losing anything. There are two distinct facts and the SCD2 shape already holds both:

- **Who first wrote this deferral** — the carried-forward pair, present unchanged on the current row *and* on the closed revision beneath it.
- **That it was corrected, and when** — the revision chain itself. Each close-and-open writes a `valid_from`/`valid_to` pair, so the boundaries of the correction are recorded as structure, not as a column value.

My recommendation would in fact have *destroyed* the first fact, which is the more important one. A deferral's stale body is usually stale *because someone specific got it wrong*; overwriting their name with the corrector's name would destroy exactly the provenance that made the original wrong — the same provenance delete-and-recreate already destroyed, and the same one the whole LB3 reversal was made to preserve. I recommended reintroducing the defect the reversal exists to fix, while arguing that doing so preserved more information.

## The process failure, recorded because it will recur

I wrote the rider while the implementing task was still in flight, and treated a sibling task's active design decision as an open question to which I should record my own recommendation. Notes are flat and immutable, so a confident-sounding note outlives its moment: a reader arriving at `e697a0ef` on `main` — where `git show main:krill/store/amend.go` still has zero occurrences of `AmendDeferral` — would find my recommendation, find no code contradicting it, and implement the amender-subject-pair behaviour, silently undoing a deliberate documented decision. The lesson for the next note-writer in this position: **when a note would restate a decision another task owns and is still making, either link to that task and stop, or verify what it shipped first.** Recording a contrary opinion is only safe once the other decision is final and you have read it.

No code changed for this correction.

**`fe4da4a5-b22b-4d85-9b12-bbbaf44ffff1`** — comment — status: noted

# CORRECTION — the `requirement` "no" conclusion stands, but its stated premise was false

**This note supersedes the `requirement` row of the table in `9cda1559-2472-4c22-a88a-91e5546906d1`.** The decision (no reparent verb for a Requirement; create-and-retire is correct) is unchanged and the rest of that note stands. What was wrong is the reason I gave, which failed the very criterion the note was built on. Re-verified against the code this time; the two corrections below are the only parts of `9cda1559` that needed changing.

## The false premise

I wrote "nothing keys on `Requirement.feature_id`". That is not true, and the note's own criterion — *does create-and-retire leave a dangling citation?* — turns on exactly this, so a false premise here would have invalidated the conclusion had anyone checked. The actual consumers, all verified:

- `krill/store/slice.go:103` (`ListRequirementsByFeatureSet`) and `slice.go:151` (`ListRequirementsByProduct`) both join `feature ON requirement.feature_id = feature.id`.
- `krill/store/requirement.go:61` and `krill/store/mediated.go:297` call `nextSiblingPosition(ctx, q, "requirement", "feature_id", parentID, scopeID)`.
- `krill/store/amend.go:287` maps `"requirement": "feature_id"` in the `parentColumn` table — the kind's declared parent column for the placement-refusal surface.

## The correct reason, which still yields "no"

The reason is not "nothing keys on `feature_id`". It is that **every one of those consumers reads the link in the child-to-parent direction, and every one of them filters the retired row out at the point of consumption** — so void-and-recreate leaves no dangling citation anywhere:

- Both `slice.go` queries carry `requirement.valid_to IS NULL` *and* `feature.valid_to IS NULL`. A voided requirement is invisible to them whatever its `feature_id` says, because the read enumerates requirements *through* their feature and the filter is on the requirement's own row. Changing the parent cannot resurrect it or orphan it; it is simply not selected.
- `nextSiblingPosition` (`position.go`) is a **create-time** helper, and its query filters `valid_to IS NULL`. Its `position` is scoped per `feature_id`, so a requirement created under a different Feature draws from a different position space entirely. Nothing outside the `requirement` table stores a requirement's parent, and no association table keys on a requirement — `entity_milestone`/`delivery_shipment` key on a Feature or LoadBearingDecision `Cn`/`LBn`, never an FR — so there is no second row anywhere holding a citation that a reparent would have to keep in sync.
- The `parentColumn` entry is a refusal surface, not a key: it is what makes `amend_requirement` say "create the requirement with the kind/parent you want, then void this one" instead of silently applying the change. That advice is correct on this corrected reasoning.

Combined with what was already right in `9cda1559` — a Requirement has no `display_number` (`nextDisplayNumber` is called only for `feature` and `load_bearing_decision`), so no rendered `Cn`-style citation exists to dangle — the conclusion holds: create the requirement under the correct Feature and `void` the old one, and the void tombstone keeps the old id resolvable so a stale citation in prose or a task body resolves to a visibly voided requirement rather than to a different live one.

One precision point worth having, since the rest of `9cda1559` leans on numbering and a reader may over-generalise: requirement **positions are reused after a void** (`nextSiblingPosition` filters `valid_to IS NULL`), unlike feature and LoadBearingDecision **display numbers, which are deliberately never reissued** (`nextDisplayNumber` counts closed rows on purpose — see its own comment, and void's number guarantee FR d38d726e (b)). That asymmetry is harmless here precisely because `position` is an ordering hint, not a citation, and only `display_number` is a citation. It is the same distinction the criterion rests on.

# ERRATUM — the `entity_milestone` DELETE count in `af5bf927`

Also a factual error in a note I recorded, found while re-verifying rather than after the fact. `af5bf927-1de5-46d6-ad27-84094d5c92ac` says grepping `DELETE FROM entity_milestone` in `krill/store/` returns "exactly one site". **It returns three**: `recut.go:433`, `recut.go:444`, and `recut.go:465`. All three are inside `MoveScope`'s transaction (the pass-2 apply loop), and all three bind `relation` to `string(MilestoneRelationDelivers)` — as `$3` in the single-container delete at `:433` and the inlined literal at `:444`/`:465`, the latter two scoped to the milepebble cuts of the source container.

**The conclusion of `af5bf927` is unaffected and remains the operative finding:** every `DELETE FROM entity_milestone` in the package lives in `MoveScope`, and every one of them is hard-scoped to `relation = 'delivers'`. So a `must_not_foreclose` row still has no correction path at all, and the recommended `WithdrawAssociation` withdrawal column still stands. Only the count was wrong; the claim it supported does not change. Worth stating precisely here rather than leaving a wrong number in a first-class note, since the sentence reads as an exhaustive count and someone could check it.

No code changed for this correction.
